clue.text: Does Germany's award make press angry?

parts.note: to press clothes is to iron them
cross is an everyday word for angry

explanation.surface: A question whether a German medal would infuriate the newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Does' belongs to the definition: the medal 'does' make the pair of words when read as a verb plus an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the German military decoration for bravery, first awarded in Prussia.

clue.text: Mutual action is the new party line

indicators.note: the new suggests a fresh version, so the letters of party line are made anew

explanation.surface: Cooperation is now the official policy of the party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'party line' looks like policy; 'the new' makes a fresh arrangement of its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Interplay is reciprocal effect, two things working on each other.

clue.text: Had a row? Nothing to an anarchist!

parts.note: O looks like zero, nothing
an gives the article a
red is used for a revolutionary or left-wing extremist

explanation.surface: Did someone have an argument? It means nothing to a revolutionary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Had a row' sounds like an argument but means rowed a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: Propelled a boat with oars, i.e. rowed.

clue.text: It's getting harder after dismissal, like, without money

indicators.note: after puts the remaining letters behind the dismissal word

parts.note: a congé is a dismissal or permission to leave

indicators.note: without means outside, so the like word goes round the money

parts.note: as means like
L stands for pound, the unit of money

explanation.surface: Things get tougher once you've been sacked and are broke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' is used in its old sense of outside: AS goes round L to make ALS.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that sets or solidifies, turning from liquid into a firmer mass.

clue.text: Found too much cloud cover

parts.note: over as a prefix means too much, as in overdo
to found metal is to cast it in a mould

explanation.surface: A complaint that there was too much cloud found in the sky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Found' is not the past of find but the verb to found, to make by melting and moulding.
explanation.definitionFit: A sky that is overcast is entirely covered by grey layer of cloud.

clue.text: Witch-doctor has ruined a Canadian province

indicators.note: ruined means wrecked, so the letters of has are knocked into a new order

parts.note: Man. is the abbreviation for Manitoba

explanation.surface: A medicine man has ruined a part of Canada.
explanation.walkthrough: MAN is the standard abbreviation for Manitoba, a prairie province.
explanation.definitionFit: A tribal healer who communicates with spirits, a medicine man.

clue.text: Put out sugar for a butterfly

indicators.note: put out suggests disturbed or upset, so the letters of sugar are disturbed into a new order

explanation.surface: An instruction to leave sugar out to attract butterflies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put out' looks like setting the sugar down; it signals that the letters of SUGAR are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The argus is a kind of brown or blue butterfly marked with eyespots.

clue.text: Charges with public burden of its gas output

indicators.note: output suggests something produced afresh, so the letters of its gas come out in a new order

explanation.surface: Fees imposed on the public for the gas that is produced.
explanation.walkthrough: To agist land is an old legal term for charging it with a public tax or rate.
explanation.definitionFit: Agist is a legal verb meaning to levy a rate or tax upon land.

clue.text: The fruit is stolen that means a charge

parts.note: grapes are a fruit
hot is slang for stolen goods

explanation.surface: Stolen fruit leading to a criminal charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'charge' looks like an accusation; it is a load fired from a cannon.
explanation.definitionFit: Grapeshot was a cannon load of small iron balls packed together.

clue.text: Hull's worse than Purgatory!

parts.note: split as S plus the place worse than purgatory, giving a word for a hull

explanation.surface: A jibe that the Yorkshire port of Hull is worse than Purgatory.
explanation.walkthrough: Hull is a city in Yorkshire, but here a hull is the outer casing of a seed or ship; HELL, worse than purgatory, follows the S.
explanation.definitionFit: The outer case of a nut or seed, or the body of a ship, is a casing.

clue.text: Rattigan as playwright

explanation.surface: Rattigan described in his role as a dramatist.
explanation.walkthrough: Terence Rattigan was a 20th-century English dramatist, and Terence was also a comic playwright of ancient Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: The first name of the English dramatist Rattigan, and also the Roman comic dramatist Publius Terentius Afer.

clue.text: If I marry — that will make things lively

parts.note: an is an archaic word for if, as in Shakespeare
to mate is to pair off or marry

explanation.surface: Someone hoping a wedding will liven things up.
explanation.walkthrough: AN for 'if' is an old usage still found in crosswords ('an it please you').
explanation.definitionFit: To animate is to bring vigour or life to something.

clue.text: This way over the Berkshire Downs

definitions.text: This way over the Berkshire Downs

parts.words: This way over the Berkshire Downs
parts.note: the clue asks for the word that, with 'way' added, names the ancient track along the chalk hills of Berkshire

explanation.surface: Directions for a walk across the hills of southern England.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ridgeway is a prehistoric track running along the Berkshire Downs, chalk hills west of London; the answer plus 'way' names it, and it is also a long raised strip of high ground.
explanation.definitionFit: A long narrow stretch of high ground, like the crest the old track follows.

clue.text: Make a good diagram of House of Churchill

parts.note: a chart is a diagram or map
well can mean good, as in 'all is well'

explanation.surface: Instruction to draw a fine plan of Churchill's home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make a' is link material; read 'diagram' as the noun and 'good' as the adverb that follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: Chartwell in Kent was Winston Churchill's family home from 1924 until his death.

clue.text: Not inclined to be languid

explanation.surface: Someone with no wish to be lazy.
explanation.walkthrough: LIST is an old word for desire or inclination, so the answer literally means lacking inclination.
explanation.definitionFit: Without the archaic 'list' (desire), hence unwilling; and also lacking energy, limp and lethargic.

clue.text: Under sergeant-major each member has weapons

indicators.note: in a down entry under places the remaining pieces below the abbreviation

parts.note: all can stand for each, every one
an arm is a limb or member
has can be contracted to 's

explanation.surface: Every soldier serving under a sergeant-major carries a gun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Under' works because the answer is written downwards, so the rest sits below SM.
explanation.definitionFit: Small arms are firearms carried by one person, such as rifles and pistols.

clue.text: It's smart to call in the County Council

indicators.note: in tells us one piece goes inside the other, the call sitting within the council

parts.note: CC is the standard abbreviation for County Council
hi is a call or greeting

explanation.surface: Advice that it is fashionable to drop in at the local council offices.
explanation.walkthrough: HI goes inside CC; 'It's' and 'to' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: Stylish and elegant, as a well-dressed person is described as fashionable.

clue.text: Feature article about Song of the Earth?

parts.note: the chin is a facial feature
a is the indefinite article
c is short for circa, about
a lay is a song or ballad

explanation.surface: A newspaper feature on a musical work about the planet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Song of the Earth' suggests Mahler; the definition is 'Earth', as china clay is a kind of earth.
explanation.definitionFit: Kaolin, a fine white clay used for porcelain, is a type of earth.

clue.text: No sailor, he settles on the island

parts.note: to land is to settle or come down
Man is the Isle of Man

explanation.surface: A man, not a sailor, who comes to live on the island.
explanation.walkthrough: The Isle of Man is a self-governing island in the Irish Sea, often clued as 'island'.
explanation.definitionFit: A landsman is someone who lives on shore and knows nothing of the sea.

clue.text: He has the utmost regard for his image

definitions.text: He has the utmost regard for his image

parts.words: He has the utmost regard for his image
parts.note: an image can be an idol, a carved figure, so the man is one who worships an image rather than a vain man

explanation.surface: A vain man obsessed with how he looks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'image' looks like self-image; read it as a graven image or idol, which this person worships.
explanation.definitionFit: A worshipper of images or a fervent admirer of a hero.

clue.text: The time is indeed right

parts.note: yea is an old word for yes or indeed

explanation.surface: Someone agreeing that now is the moment.
explanation.definitionFit: A twelve-month period, a measure of elapsed duration.

clue.text: Gangsters strip it and put it back

parts.note: a band is a strip of material

indicators.note: put and back together tell us the second it is turned around
back completes the instruction that this it is written backwards

explanation.surface: Robbers stripping something and then returning it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put it back' reverses the second IT to give TI.
explanation.definitionFit: Banditti is the old Italian plural for outlaws or brigands, a robber band.

clue.text: No note on former religious devotee

parts.note: O looks like zero, so no
B is a musical note
late means former, as in the late chairman

explanation.surface: A former monk who had no knowledge of music.
explanation.definitionFit: An oblate is a layperson dedicated to monastic life.

clue.text: Fit to be extended

parts.note: long means extended in length

explanation.surface: Something fit to be stretched out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fit' is a verb: to fit in somewhere is to belong.
explanation.definitionFit: To belong is to be suited or in the proper place, to fit in.

clue.text: Henry failed initially to propagate hybrid

parts.note: Hal is a pet form of Henry, as with Shakespeare's Prince Hal

indicators.note: initially means take only the opening letter of failed

parts.note: to breed is to propagate

explanation.surface: Henry was unsuccessful in raising a crossbred plant or animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Henry' is not H here but HAL, the familiar form.
explanation.definitionFit: An offensive old term for someone of mixed descent, applied also to crossbred animals.

clue.text: Bird's' off its nut to produce this brood

indicators.note: off means removed, so the nut is taken away from the bird

parts.note: the nuthatch is a small tree-climbing bird
taken as written

explanation.surface: A bird gone mad producing chicks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off its nut' looks like crazy, but it says the bird name loses NUT.
explanation.definitionFit: A brood of chicks is what a clutch of eggs produces at one time, a hatching.

clue.text: Snake-charmer versed in Keats

explanation.surface: A snake-charmer who knows Keats's poetry well.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek legend the figure is a serpent woman who enchants men; Keats wrote a narrative poem of that title.
explanation.definitionFit: A serpent-woman who bewitches a young man, the subject of a narrative poem by Keats published in 1820.

clue.text: The lesson of many an examination

parts.note: M is a thousand in Roman numerals, hence many
an oral is a spoken examination

explanation.surface: The teaching drawn from many tests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' and 'an' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: A moral is the lesson a story teaches.

clue.text: Rent a party? There'd be an awful storm!

parts.note: rent as a past participle means torn
a do is a party

explanation.surface: Someone warning that hiring a party venue would cause a row.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rent' looks like hiring, but it is the past participle of rend, to tear.
explanation.definitionFit: A violent rotating column of wind, a twister.

clue.text: What a blow for a poet!

definitions.text: What a blow for a poet!

parts.words: What a blow for a poet!
parts.note: a blow is a wind, and the wind of southern France shares its name with a Provençal poet

explanation.surface: An exclamation of sympathy at a poet's misfortune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blow' looks like a setback; it means a wind, the strong cold north wind of southern France, also the name of the Nobel-winning poet Frédéric Mistral.
explanation.definitionFit: A cold dry northerly wind of the Rhône valley, and the surname of the Provençal Nobel laureate poet.

clue.text: Hurry as the letters need sorting

indicators.note: letters needing sorting are to be put into a new order, so the letters of the previous words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A rush because the post must be sorted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'letters' looks like mail; it means the letters of AS THE, which are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Speed or urgency, the act of rushing.

clue.text: Biology groups take £50 before start of 19 as a rule

indicators.note: before puts the pound and fifty ahead of the last piece

parts.note: genera are groups in biological classification
£ is L (from Latin libra) and 50 is L in Roman numerals
19 across is YEAR, whose first letter is Y

explanation.surface: Taxonomy costs fifty pounds before the start of the year, as usual.
explanation.walkthrough: The pound sign gives L (libra) and 50 gives another L; '19' points to another answer, whose first letter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Usually, in most cases, is what generally means.
